claim: Fyv6 (FAM192A in humans) was recently identified as a second step factor in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
source: We recently identified Fyv6 (FAM192A in humans) as a second step factor in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work and is presented as an established finding from the authors' previous research.

claim: Loss of Fyv6 results in activation of non-consensus, branch point (BP) proximal 3′ SS transcriptome-wide
source: These results show that loss of Fyv6 results in activation of non-consensus, branch point (BP) proximal 3ʹ SS transcriptome-wide.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript showing widespread changes in 3' splice site usage.

claim: A high-resolution cryo-EM structure of a yeast product complex spliceosome containing Fyv6 was determined at 2.3 Å resolution
source: To identify the molecular basis of these observations, we determined a high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of a yeast product complex spliceosome containing Fyv6 at 2.3 Å.
evidence: The manuscript describes cryo-EM data collection and processing that resulted in a 2.3 Å structure.

claim: Fyv6 is the only second step factor that contacts the Prp22 ATPase
source: The structure reveals that Fyv6 is the only second step factor that contacts the Prp22 ATPase
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure showing direct interactions between Fyv6 and Prp22.

claim: Fyv6 binding is mutually exclusive with that of the first step factor Yju2
source: that Fyv6 binding is mutually exclusive with that of the first step factor Yju2
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing overlapping binding sites on Syf1 for Fyv6 and Yju2.

claim: Yju2/Fyv6 exchange facilitates exon ligation
source: The combined transcriptomic, structural, and genetic studies allow us to propose a model in which Yju2/Fyv6 exchange facilitates exon ligation
evidence: This is a model proposed based on integration of multiple types of data including structural and genetic evidence.

claim: Fyv6 promotes usage of consensus, BP distal 3′ SS
source: Fyv6 promotes usage of consensus, BP distal 3ʹ SS
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing activation of BP proximal sites when Fyv6 is deleted, and biochemical assays showing reduced efficiency at BP distal sites.

claim: Pre-mRNA splicing is catalyzed by a large macromolecular complex called the spliceosome
source: Precursor messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) splicing is catalyzed by a large macromolecular complex called the spliceosome.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the splicing machinery.

claim: Spliceosomes are composed of five small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs)
source: Spliceosomes are composed of five small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), each composed of a small nuclear RNA (snRNA; U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6) and several different protein splicing factors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about spliceosome composition.

claim: The splicing reaction is carried out in two sequential transesterification reactions
source: The splicing reaction itself is carried out in two sequential transesterification reactions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the splicing mechanism, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The 5′ splice site is cleaved during formation of an intron lariat in the first step
source: First, the 5ʹ splice site (5ʹ SS) is cleaved during formation of an intron lariat (first step).
evidence: This describes the first step of splicing, which is established knowledge.

claim: The intron lariat is removed simultaneously with exon ligation at the 3′ SS in the second step
source: Second, the intron lariat is removed simultaneously with exon ligation at the 3ʹ SS (second step).
evidence: This describes the second step of splicing, which is established knowledge.

claim: fyv6Δ upf1Δ double mutant strain showed reduced growth at 30°C and cold-sensitive (cs) and temperature-sensitive (ts) phenotypes relative to a upf1Δ control strain
source: Consistent with results from fyv6Δ strains, the fyv6Δ upf1Δ double mutant strain also showed reduced growth at 30°C and cold-sensitive (cs) and temperature-sensitive (ts) phenotypes relative to a upf1Δ control strain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Many more changes in splicing were observed in the fyv6Δ upf1Δ strain relative to the fyv6Δ strain
source: As expected, many more changes in splicing were observed in the fyv6Δ upf1Δ strain relative to the fyv6Δ strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing the two strains, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Loss of Fyv6 results in many mRNA isoforms being substrates for NMD
source: This is consistent with many mRNA isoforms generated due to loss of Fyv6 being substrates for NMD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that more splicing changes are detected when NMD is suppressed (upf1Δ background).

claim: Loss of Fyv6 resulted in a number of changes in gene expression with many non-intron-containing genes also being up- or downregulated
source: Loss of Fyv6 resulted in a number of changes in gene expression with many non-intron-containing genes also being up- or downregulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At all temperatures, changes in alternative 3′ SS usage were observed in the fyv6Δ strain relative to the FYV6 background
source: At all temperatures, we see changes in alternative 3ʹ SS usage in the fyv6Δ strain relative to the FYV6 background.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis at different temperatures.

claim: Use of the alternative 3′ SS in the first intron of the SUS1 transcript was detected as previously reported
source: For example, we detected use of the alternative 3ʹ SS in the first intron of the SUS1 transcript as we previously reported (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; Lipinski et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and confirmed by previous publication.

claim: Increased use of a cryptic, non-consensus GAG 3′ SS in the first, but not second, intron of the YOS1 transcript was observed in the fyv6Δ datasets
source: We also saw increased use of a cryptic, non-consensus GAG 3ʹ SS in the first, but not second, intron of the YOS1 transcript in the fyv6Δ datasets and confirmed this result by RT-PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and confirmed by RT-PCR.

claim: The majority of alternative 5′ SS were used with equal efficiencies in the WT and fyv6Δ strains
source: However, the majority of these alternative 5ʹ SS were used with equal efficiencies in the WT and fyv6Δ strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by FAnS analysis of alternative 5' SS shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The strains temperature shifted to 16°C had the largest number of changes due to FYV6 deletion
source: The strains temperature shifted to 16°C had the largest number of changes due to FYV6 deletion and the strains shifted to 37°C the least.
evidence: This is supported by counting alternative splicing events at different temperatures shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The temperature shift to 16°C caused an increase in the numbers of both alternative 3′ SS and retained intron events detected
source: The temperature shift to 16°C caused an increase in the numbers of both alternative 3ʹ SS and retained intron events detected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the bar chart in Figure 1C.

claim: The changes in alternative 3′ SS used at each temperature were mostly unique with few events detected under all three conditions
source: The changes in alternative 3ʹ SS used at each temperature were mostly unique with few events detected under all three conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 1D.

claim: 61 different RNAs (~20% of introns) changed splicing patterns due to loss of Fyv6
source: Collectively, we observed that 61 different RNAs (~20% of introns) changed splicing patterns due to loss of Fyv6.
evidence: This is a summary of the RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: For many mRNAs with changed splicing patterns, multiple different 3′ SS were detected being used
source: For many of these mRNAs, we detected multiple different 3ʹ SS being used.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: Changes in alternative 3′ SS usage were confirmed for both ribosomal protein gene (RPG) and non-RPG transcripts at all conditions
source: These results confirm changes in alternative 3ʹ SS usage for both ribosomal protein gene (RPG) and non-RPG transcripts at all conditions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in the box plots in Figure 1E.

claim: No significant differences between RPG and non-RPG splicing were detected with FAnS analysis
source: We could not detect any significant differences between RPG and non-RPG splicing with this analysis
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the FAnS ratios.

claim: Differences in gene expression and splicing efficiencies between RPG and non-RPG classes are not correlated with alternative 3′ SS usage
source: suggesting that differences in gene expression and splicing efficiencies between these two classes are not correlated with alternative 3ʹ SS usage
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant differences in FAnS analysis between RPG and non-RPG.

claim: Fyv6 plays a critical role in defining mRNA isoform production in yeast, particularly under non-optimal growth conditions such as temperature stress
source: Combined these results show that Fyv6 plays a critical role in defining mRNA isoform production in yeast, particularly under non-optimal growth conditions such as temperature stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data showing widespread changes in splicing, especially at non-optimal temperatures.

claim: The majority of the alternative 3′ SS arising from Fyv6 deletion are upstream of the canonical 3′ SS
source: This analysis shows that the majority of the alternative 3ʹ SS arising from Fyv6 deletion are upstream (Figure 2A, pink points above the diagonal).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot in Figure 2A.

claim: Most alternative 3′ SS are found within ~40 nt upstream of the canonical site
source: When these alternative 3ʹ SS are mapped according to their nucleotide distance from the canonical site, most of these are found within ~40 nt upstream (Figure 2B, purple violin).
evidence: This is shown in the violin plot in Figure 2B.

claim: The highest density of alternative 3′ SS sites is ≤20 nt from the BP for transcripts with the highest FAnS ratios
source: Plotting these alternative 3ʹ SS sites relative to their distance from the annotated BP reveals that the highest density of sites is ≤20 nt from the BP for transcripts with the highest FAnS ratios (Figure 2C, purple violin).
evidence: This is shown in the violin plot in Figure 2C.

claim: A small number of alternative 3′ SS detected in the Fyv6 datasets are located upstream of the annotated BP, suggesting activation of an alternative BP and 3′ SS
source: Indeed, a small number of alternative 3ʹ SS detected in the Fyv6 datasets are located upstream of the annotated BP, suggesting activation of an alternative BP and 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of alternative 3' SS upstream of the annotated BP in the data.

claim: The changes in splicing are predominantly due to usage of alternative 3′ SS located between the annotated BP and canonical 3′ SS
source: However, we believe that the changes are predominantly due to usage of alternative 3ʹ SS located between the annotated BP and canonical 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of alternative 3' SS relative to the BP and canonical 3' SS.

claim: Fyv6 is important for splicing of 3′ SS located distant from the BP
source: The above results suggest that Fyv6 is important for splicing of 3ʹ SS located distant from the BP.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing activation of BP proximal sites when Fyv6 is deleted.

claim: Loss of Fyv6 has minimal impact on exon ligation when BP to 3′ SS distances are short (9–15 nt)
source: While loss of Fyv6 has minimal impact on exon ligation when BP to 3ʹ SS distances are short (9–15 nt), exon ligation efficiency decreases significantly at distances of 21 nt or greater.
evidence: This is supported by primer extension analysis of ACT1-CUP1 reporters with varying BP-3'SS distances shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Exon ligation efficiency decreases significantly at BP to 3′ SS distances of 21 nt or greater when Fyv6 is absent
source: While loss of Fyv6 has minimal impact on exon ligation when BP to 3ʹ SS distances are short (9–15 nt), exon ligation efficiency decreases significantly at distances of 21 nt or greater.
evidence: This is supported by primer extension analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No evidence of cryptic BP usage was detected in the ACT1-CUP1 reporter assays
source: In addition, we do not see evidence of cryptic BP usage in these assays.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the primer extension results.

claim: The ACT1-CUP1 reporter result is consistent with the RNA-seq analysis and supports a function for Fyv6 in facilitating splicing at BP distal 3′ SS
source: This result is consistent with the RNA-seq analysis and supports a function for Fyv6 in facilitating splicing at BP distal 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the reporter assay results with the RNA-seq data.

claim: For alternative 3′ SS located upstream of the canonical 3′ SS, much greater sequence variability was observed relative to the canonical site
source: For sites located upstream of the canonical 3ʹ SS, we observed much greater sequence variability relative to the canonical site.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence logos in Figure 2G.

claim: Increased use of highly variable 3′ SS including those with atypical HAU and BG motifs was detected
source: We detected increased use of highly variable 3ʹ SS including those with atypical HAU (H=A,C,U) and BG (B=C,U,G) motifs and confirmed generation of new RNA isoforms for several of these by RT-PCR (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and RT-PCR confirmation.

claim: Increased use of variable 3′ SS was also observed when the second step factor PRP18 was deleted
source: Increased use of variable 3ʹ SS was also observed when the second step factor PRP18 was deleted (Roy et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data from another study.

claim: The subset of RNAs most impacted by splicing factor deletion appear to be different between Fyv6 and Prp18
source: However, the subset of RNAs most impacted by splicing factor deletion appear to be different.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the affected transcripts in fyv6Δ versus prp18Δ datasets.

claim: Changes in 3′ SS usage for UBC12, MAF1, MUD1, PHO85, SPT14, or YCL002C transcripts reported for prp18Δ were not detected in the fyv6Δ datasets
source: For example, we were not able to detect changes in 3ʹ SS usage for the UBC12, MAF1, MUD1, PHO85, SPT14, or YCL002C transcripts in the fyv6Δ datasets as was reported for prp18Δ (not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the fyv6Δ RNA-seq data and comparison with published prp18Δ data.

claim: Prp18 and Fyv6 likely have transcript-specific effects on splicing outcomes
source: Prp18 and Fyv6 likely have transcript-specific effects on splicing outcomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different transcripts are affected by deletion of these two factors.

claim: Fyv6 is a second step splicing factor that facilitates usage of consensus sites located distal to the BP in vivo
source: Combined our results strongly support Fyv6 as a second step splicing factor that facilitates usage of consensus sites located distal to the BP in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined RNA-seq and biochemical data.

claim: Previous structures of the yeast P complex spliceosome were solved with resolutions at the core ranging from 3.3 Å to 3.7 Å
source: Previous structures of the yeast P complex spliceosome were solved with resolutions at the core ranging from 3.3 Å to 3.7 Å (Bai et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Wilkinson et al., 2017)
evidence: This is based on published cryo-EM structures.

claim: Peripheral components such as the Prp22 helicase, U2 snRNP, and Prp19 complex (NTC) in previous P complex structures were at much lower resolutions (5–10 Å) that precluded detailed investigation
source: and with peripheral components such as the Prp22 helicase, U2 snRNP, and Prp19 complex (NTC) at much lower resolutions (5–10 Å) that precluded detailed investigation.
evidence: This is based on published cryo-EM structures.

claim: P complex was purified by stalling spliceosome disassembly with a dominant negative mutant of Prp22 (S635A) defective in mRNA release
source: To improve the resolution, we purified P complex as previously described by stalling spliceosome disassembly with a dominant negative mutant of Prp22 (S635A) defective in mRNA release (Schwer and Meszaros, 2000; Wilkinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the method used for P complex purification, based on published approaches.

claim: The P complex structure was resolved to 2.3 Å within the catalytic core
source: However, by collecting a much larger cryo-EM dataset on a more modern electron detector, we were able to resolve the structure to 2.3 Å within the catalytic core
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data collection and processing.

claim: Peripheral components were visualized at resolutions from 3.0 Å to 3.7 Å
source: as well as visualize peripheral components at resolutions from 3.0 Å to 3.7 Å (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–4; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on focused refinement of cryo-EM data.

claim: This is the highest resolution spliceosome structure to date
source: This is the highest resolution spliceosome structure to date.
evidence: This is a comparison with all previously published spliceosome structures.

claim: The high-quality density at the active site shows the positions of bases unambiguously, confirming the manner of the non-Watson-Crick base pairing that mediates 3′ SS recognition
source: The high-quality density at the active site shows the positions of bases unambiguously, confirming the manner of the non-Watson-Crick base pairing that mediates 3ʹ SS recognition (Liu et al., 2017; Wilkinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density and comparison with previous structures.

claim: Monovalent ions bound at the active site were previously shown to be important during the first step of splicing
source: Monovalent ions bound at the active site were previously shown to be important during the first step of splicing (Wilkinson et al., 2021)
evidence: This is based on a previous publication.

claim: The positions of monovalent ions are preserved after exon ligation
source: and our data indicate that the positions of these ions are preserved after exon ligation.
evidence: This is based on observation of ion positions in the P complex structure.

claim: The density shows a metal ion, likely potassium, that bridges the base pair between +1G of the 5′ SS and –1G of the 3′ SS
source: Additionally, the density also shows a metal ion, likely potassium, that bridges the base pair between +1G of the 5ʹ SS and –1G of the 3ʹ SS (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density at the active site.

claim: The second step splicing factor Prp22 is resolved at 3.0 Å resolution, allowing atomic interpretation for the first time
source: The second step splicing factor Prp22 is resolved at 3.0 Å resolution, allowing atomic interpretation for the first time (Figure 3B and later figures).
evidence: This is based on focused refinement of the Prp22 region.

claim: Bases 13–21 of the 3′ exon are visible between the two RecA domains of Prp22 consistent with biochemical footprinting data
source: Bases 13–21 of the 3ʹ exon are visible between the two RecA domains of Prp22 consistent with biochemical footprinting data (Schwer, 2008; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with published biochemical data.

claim: The S635A mutation used to stall P complex is visible in the structure
source: The S635A mutation used to stall P complex is also visible
evidence: This is based on observation in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The origin of defective mRNA release due to the S635A mutation is not apparent from the structure
source: however, the origin of defective mRNA release due to this mutation is not apparent (Schwer and Meszaros, 2000).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with published functional data.

claim: The loop containing S635A is in a similar conformation in this structure and in the structure of WT human Prp22
source: The loop containing S635A is in a similar conformation in this structure and in the structure of WT human Prp22 (Felisberto-Rodrigues et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a published crystal structure.

claim: Part of the extensive N-terminal domain of Prp22 is resolved and constitutes a long helix that bridges between the Prp22 RecA2 domain and the C-terminal domain of Cwc22
source: Part of the extensive N-terminal domain of Prp22 is resolved and constitutes a long helix that bridges between the Prp22 RecA2 domain and the C-terminal domain of Cwc22; this helix was unassigned in previous P complex structures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with previous structures.

claim: A new data-driven regularization strategy was used to improve the resolution of the peripheral, flexible regions
source: To improve the resolution of the peripheral, flexible regions, we used a new data-driven regularization strategy (Kimanius et al., 2024) that allows focused refinements of much smaller domains than previously possible (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This describes a new computational method used for cryo-EM data processing.

claim: Combined with AlphaFold2-assisted modeling, more accurate models for the U2 snRNP, NTC, U5 Sm ring, and Cwc22 N-terminal domains were obtained
source: Combined with AlphaFold2-assisted modeling, we were able to obtain more accurate models for the U2 snRNP, NTC, U5 Sm ring, and Cwc22 N-terminal domains.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used.

claim: The model for the NTC within the P complex is similar to the previous model for the NTC within C and Ci complexes
source: Our model for the NTC within the P complex is similar to our previous model for the NTC within C and Ci complexes (Wilkinson et al., 2021; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current structure with previously published structures.

claim: A star-shaped density coordinated by several conserved lysines from Clf1 and Ntc20 was observed, which was modeled as inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6)
source: Notably however, we observed a star-shaped density coordinated by several conserved lysines from Clf1 and Ntc20, which we were able to model as inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density and modeling.

claim: The same IP6 density, at lower resolution, is visible in the C complex
source: The same density, at lower resolution, is visible in the C complex (Wilkinson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously published structure.

claim: A distinct, separate IP6 molecule had previously been observed within all catalytic spliceosomes between the Bact and P complex stages coordinated by Prp8 and (for C* and P complexes) Slu7
source: A distinct, separate IP6 molecule had previously been observed within all catalytic spliceosomes between the Bact and P complex stages coordinated by Prp8 and (for C* and P complexes) Slu7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on previously published structures.

claim: The NTC-bound IP6 is not believed to be essential for splicing since deletion of the Clf1 tetratricopeptide repeat that coordinates IP6 does not result in growth or splicing phenotypes in yeast
source: We do not believe that the NTC-bound IP6 is essential for splicing since deletion of the Clf1 tetratricopeptide repeat that coordinates IP6 does not result in growth or splicing phenotypes in yeast and Ntc20 is a nonessential splicing factor (Chen et al., 2001; Chung et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on published genetic data.

claim: It is possible that IP6 may regulate splicing in some manner via interactions with both Prp8 and the NTC
source: Nonetheless, it is possible that IP6 may regulate splicing in some manner via interactions with both Prp8 and the NTC.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: Three connected long α-helices were unambiguously assigned to Fyv6
source: We were able to unambiguously assign three, connected long α-helices to Fyv6 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density and model building.

claim: These Fyv6 helices were visible in previous cryo-EM reconstructions of yeast C* and P complexes but were either unassigned or misassigned
source: These helices were visible in previous cryo-EM reconstructions of yeast C* and P complexes but were either unassigned or misassigned.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published structures.

claim: In cases of misassigned densities, Fyv6 was previously attributed to the C-terminal domain of the first step factor Yju2
source: In the cases of misassigned densities, Fyv6 was previously attributed to the C-terminal domain of the first step factor Yju2 (Wilkinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously published structure.

claim: Yju2 also has an elongated helical architecture and adopts a similar position on C complex and the post-P complex intron lariat spliceosome (ILS)
source: Yju2 also has an elongated helical architecture and adopts a similar position on C complex (Wilkinson et al., 2021) and the post-P complex intron lariat spliceosome (ILS) (Wan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on previously published structures.

claim: The Yju2 C-terminus is a better fit than Fyv6 for densities in B*, C, and ILS complexes
source: We closely inspected the density from previously determined spliceosome structures and concluded that the Yju2 C-terminus is still a better fit than Fyv6 for densities in B*, C, and ILS complexes
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published cryo-EM densities.

claim: Fyv6 is a better fit than Yju2 for densities in C* and P complexes
source: whereas Fyv6 is a better fit than Yju2 for densities in C* and P complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of cryo-EM densities using ModelAngelo.

claim: The position of Fyv6 seems to be characteristic of a second step conformation of the spliceosome
source: Therefore, this position of Fyv6 seems to be characteristic of a second step conformation of the spliceosome
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of Fyv6 in C* and P complexes but not earlier complexes.

claim: The position of Fyv6 is consistent with the position of its distant human homolog FAM192A in the human pre-C* complex
source: and consistent with the position of its distant human homolog FAM192A in the human pre-C* complex (Zhan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a published human spliceosome structure.

claim: Fyv6 makes a multitude of interactions with essential splicing factors
source: Fyv6 makes a multitude of interactions with essential splicing factors (Figures 3B and 4E–G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: One conserved region of Fyv6 is the N-terminus with an FVSE motif
source: One conserved region of Fyv6 is the N-terminus with an FVSE motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment of Fyv6 homologs.

claim: The FVSE motif forms a 'hook' that interacts with a hydrophobic patch on the surface of the Prp22 RecA2 domain
source: This motif forms a 'hook' that interacts with a hydrophobic patch on the surface of the Prp22 RecA2 domain, where it also forms hydrogen bonds by β-sheet augmentation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The hook is followed by three α-helices
source: The hook is followed by three α-helices.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The start of helix 2 sits on top of the intron between the BP and the active site docked 3′ SS, where it may act as a steric block to prevent 3′ SS undocking and promote exon ligation
source: The start of helix 2 sits on top of the intron between the BP and the active site docked 3ʹ SS, where it may act as a steric block to prevent 3ʹ SS undocking and promote exon ligation (Figure 4F; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with a previous publication.

claim: Helix 2 contains a patch of conserved arginines that form salt bridges with Asp317 and Glu318 of Slu7
source: Helix 2 also contains a patch of conserved arginines that form salt bridges with Asp317 and Glu318 of Slu7 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The linker between helices 2 and 3 interacts with the NTC component Cef1
source: The linker between helices 2 and 3 interacts with the NTC component Cef1
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Helix 3 interacts with NTC component Syf1
source: and helix 3 interacts with NTC component Syf1 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The binding interface with Syf1 overlaps with the Syf1/Yju2 interaction in the C complex
source: The binding interface with Syf1 overlaps with the Syf1/Yju2 interaction in the C complex (Wilkinson et al., 2021), suggesting these interactions are mutually exclusive (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the P complex structure with the C complex structure.

claim: Fyv6 provides a direct link between the Prp22 ATPase, NTC components, and other essential splicing factors over a distance of ~100 Å
source: Fyv6 thus provides a direct link between the Prp22 ATPase, NTC components, and other essential splicing factors over a distance of ~100 Å.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural observations.

claim: By 3D classification, three states of the P complex spliceosome were resolved
source: By 3D classification, we were able to resolve a total of three states of the P complex spliceosome (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is based on 3D classification of cryo-EM particles.

claim: State I, represented by 51% of particles, is the most complete and has all the described factors visible, including a stably docked 3′ SS
source: State I, represented by 51% of particles, is the most complete and has all the above-described factors visible, including a stably docked 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is based on 3D classification and analysis of the resulting maps.

claim: State II, represented by 20% of particles, is similar to state I but lacks density for the N-terminal half of the second step factor Slu7
source: State II, represented by 20% of particles, is similar to state I but lacks density for the N-terminal half of the second step factor Slu7.
evidence: This is based on 3D classification and analysis of the resulting maps.

claim: In state II, the endonuclease-like domain of Prp8, to which the N-terminal domain of Slu7 binds, is correspondingly shifted
source: The endonuclease-like domain of Prp8, to which this domain of Slu7 binds, is correspondingly shifted.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the state II map.

claim: State II retains strong density for the 3′ SS, suggesting the N-terminal regions of Slu7 are not involved in maintaining 3′ SS docking after exon ligation
source: Interestingly, this state retains strong density for the 3ʹ SS, suggesting the N-terminal regions of Slu7 are not involved in maintaining 3ʹ SS docking after exon ligation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the 3' SS is docked even when the N-terminal domain of Slu7 is not visible.

claim: State III, containing 29% of particles, entirely lacks density for the second step factors Slu7, Prp18, and Fyv6
source: Finally, state III, containing 29% of particles, entirely lacks density for the second step factors Slu7, Prp18, and Fyv6.
evidence: This is based on 3D classification and analysis of the resulting maps.

claim: In state III, Prp17 and the RNase H domain of Prp8 are still present but are weaker than in States I and II, suggesting they are more flexible in state III
source: Prp17 and the RNase H domain of Prp8 are still present but are weaker than in States I and II, suggesting they are more flexible in state III.
evidence: This is inferred from the weaker density for these components in state III.

claim: In state III, most of Prp22 can be observed with weaker density except for the C-terminal domain that interacts with Prp8, which lacks density entirely
source: Most of Prp22 can still be observed with weaker density except for the C-terminal domain that interacts with Prp8, which lacks density entirely.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the state III map.

claim: State III lacks density for the 3′ SS but has density for the 3′ exon, suggesting it is post-catalytic and represents a state after loss of second step factors and undocking of the 3′ SS from the catalytic core
source: Importantly, state III also lacks density for the 3ʹ SS but has density for the 3ʹ exon, suggesting it is indeed post-catalytic and represents a state after loss of second step factors and undocking of the 3ʹ SS from the catalytic core.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of 3' SS density but presence of 3' exon density in state III.

claim: The coincidence of loss of Fyv6 with loss of Prp18 and Slu7 reinforces the notion that these three factors act together and are important for 3′ SS docking
source: The coincidence of loss of Fyv6 with loss of Prp18 and Slu7 reinforces the notion that these three factors act together and are important for 3ʹ SS docking, maintaining the 3ʹ SS in the active site after exon ligation, and for stabilization of Prp17, Prp22, and the RNase H domain of Prp8.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all three factors are absent in state III, which also lacks a docked 3' SS.

claim: Five truncation mutants of Fyv6 were designed using the cryo-EM structure
source: To determine the functionally critical regions and interactions of Fyv6, we used the cryo-EM structure to design five truncation mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design based on structural information.

claim: All of the N-terminal truncation mutations could suppress the cs or ts phenotypes to some degree
source: All of the N-terminal truncation mutations could suppress the cs or ts phenotypes to some degree.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A strain with the complete deletion of the conserved hook domain that interacts with Prp22 (Δ1–23) grew similarly to the strain expressing WT Fyv6
source: Surprisingly, a strain with the complete deletion of the conserved hook domain that interacts with Prp22 (Δ1–23) grew similarly to the strain expressing WT Fyv6.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The N-terminal truncation mutants showed no evidence for changes in SUS1 splicing
source: In addition to suppression of the fyv6Δ growth phenotype, the N-terminal truncation mutants also showed no evidence for changes in SUS1 splicing (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The N-terminal region of Fyv6 composed of the hook domain and the first α-helix is not required for suppression of either the temperature sensitivity or splicing phenotypes observed when Fyv6 is lost
source: The N-terminal region of Fyv6 composed of the hook domain and the first α-helix is not required for suppression of either the temperature sensitivity or splicing phenotypes observed when Fyv6 is lost despite its conservation and interactions with critical splicing factors (Prp8, Prp22, and Slu7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the growth and RT-PCR data for N-terminal truncation mutants.

claim: The Δ134–173 truncation was able to suppress the cs and ts phenotypes, indicating that the predicted NLS is not essential
source: For the C-terminal truncations, the Δ134–173 truncation was also able to suppress the cs and ts phenotypes, indicating that the predicted NLS is also not essential (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Δ134–173 mutant grew more poorly at 16°C than did the Δ1–16 and Δ1–23 truncations and showed some evidence of alternative 3′ SS usage in SUS1
source: However, this mutant grew more poorly at 16°C than did the Δ1–16 and Δ1–23 truncations and showed some evidence of alternative 3ʹ SS usage in SUS1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on growth assays and RT-PCR shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The Δ103–173 truncation strain phenocopied the fyv6Δ strain and grew poorly at 37°C and was dead at 23°C or 16°C
source: The largest effects were seen when the C-terminus was truncated further. The Δ103–173 truncation strain phenocopied the fyv6Δ strain and grew poorly at 37°C and was dead at 23°C or 16°C (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RT-PCR showed increased use of the alternative 3′ SS in SUS1 with the Δ103–173 truncation
source: Additionally, RT-PCR showed increased use of the alternative 3ʹ SS in SUS1 with this truncation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The abundance of the N-terminally epitope-tagged Δ103–173 variant was much lower than the other Fyv6 variants
source: In all cases, we could detect protein; however, the abundance of the N-terminally epitope-tagged Δ103–173 variant was much lower than the others.
evidence: This is based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The C-terminally tagged Δ103–173 protein expressed at much higher levels but also failed to suppress the cs and ts phenotypes
source: Therefore, we also constructed a C-terminally epitope-tagged version of Δ103–173 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). The C-terminally tagged protein expressed at much higher levels but also failed to suppress the cs and ts phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on western blot and growth assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The C-terminal region of Fyv6 that includes a portion of α-helix 3 and the Syf1 interaction domain is critical for function
source: These data suggest that the C-terminal region of Fyv6 that includes a portion of α-helix 3 and the Syf1 interaction domain is critical for function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the truncation mutant analysis.

claim: Loss of the Fyv6-interacting domain on Syf1 would phenocopy fyv6Δ
source: To obtain additional evidence for the importance of the Fyv6/Syf1 interaction, we created a syf1Δ shuffle strain containing WT Fyv6 and expressed C-terminal Syf1 truncations (Figure 5D). We hypothesized that loss of the Fyv6-interacting domain on Syf1 would phenocopy fyv6Δ.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by creating Syf1 truncation mutants.

claim: Loss of the Fyv6-interacting region in Syf1 Δ778–859 and Δ634–859 mutants resulted in either modest (Δ778–859) or severe (Δ634–859) cs and ts phenotypes
source: We observed just this effect. Loss of the Fyv6-interacting region in Syf1 Δ778–859 and Δ634–859 mutants resulted in either modest (Δ778–859) or severe (Δ634–859) cs and ts phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Syf1 Δ778–859 and Δ634–859 truncation mutants triggered use of the alternative 3′ SS in SUS1
source: In addition, these Syf1 truncation mutants also triggered use of the alternative 3ʹ SS in SUS1 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR shown in Figure 5F.

claim: If the Δ778–859 and Δ817–859 Syf1 mutants are expressed in a fyv6Δ background, it results in suppression of the fyv6Δ ts phenotype
source: Interestingly, if the Δ778–859 and Δ817–859 Syf1 mutants are expressed in a fyv6Δ background, it results in suppression of the fyv6Δ ts phenotype (Figure 5G; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The SUS1 alternative 3′ SS is still used when Δ778–859 and Δ817–859 Syf1 mutants are expressed in a fyv6Δ background
source: However, the SUS1 alternative 3ʹ SS is still used (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR shown in Figure 5H.

claim: ts phenotype suppression and triggering usage of the alternative 3′ SS in SUS1 are separable processes
source: This indicates that ts phenotype suppression and triggering usage of the alternative 3ʹ SS in SUS1 are separable processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Syf1 truncations can suppress ts phenotype but not SUS1 splicing defects in fyv6Δ background.

claim: In the absence of Fyv6, Syf1 may inappropriately bind Yju2 during exon ligation
source: When considered together, these results likely originate from mutually exclusive Fyv6/Syf1 and Yju2/Syf1 interactions. It is possible that in the absence of Fyv6, Syf1 inappropriately binds Yju2 during exon ligation.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the genetic data.

claim: The presence of Yju2 during the second step could lead to growth defects that are suppressed when the Yju2-binding site on Syf1 is deleted
source: The presence of Yju2 during the second step could then lead to growth defects that are suppressed when the Yju2-binding site on Syf1 is deleted.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the suppression of ts phenotype by Syf1 truncations in fyv6Δ background.

claim: The absence of Fyv6 could perturb the equilibrium between the first and second step conformations of the spliceosome and result in favoring of the first step
source: Alternatively or in addition, the absence of Fyv6 could perturb the equilibrium between the first and second step conformations of the spliceosome and result in favoring of the first step (Liu et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is an alternative model proposed to explain the genetic data, based on published work.

claim: Loss of this equilibrium could lead to growth defects that are suppressed by destabilization of the first step conformation by removing a binding site for Yju2 on Syf1 and restoring the equilibrium
source: Loss of this equilibrium could lead to growth defects that are suppressed by destabilization of the first step conformation by removing a binding site for Yju2 on Syf1 and restoring the equilibrium.
evidence: This is part of the alternative model proposed to explain the genetic data.

claim: Truncation of Syf1 suppresses growth defects but not SUS1 splicing defects since Fyv6 function is still needed during the second step
source: In both cases, truncation of Syf1 suppresses growth defects but not SUS1 splicing defects since Fyv6 function is still needed during the second step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic data.

claim: A genetic screen was carried out to detect spontaneously arising suppressors that can correct temperature-dependent growth defects
source: To gain additional insights into Fyv6 function, we carried out a genetic screen to detect spontaneously arising suppressors that can correct temperature-dependent growth defects (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: This method has previously been used to illuminate many aspects of spliceosome biochemistry and non-silent mutations within splicing factors are likely causative for suppression
source: This method has previously been used to illuminate many aspects of spliceosome biochemistry and non-silent mutations within splicing factors are likely causative for suppression (Montemayor et al., 2014; Kuhn and Brow, 2000; Brow, 2019).
evidence: This is based on published work using similar genetic screens.

claim: All of the picked colonies were able to suppress growth defects at 37°C, and many also suppressed the cs phenotype at 23°C
source: A subset of picked colonies were then tested for suppression of the ts phenotype. All of these colonies were able to suppress growth defects at 37°C, and many also suppressed the cs phenotype at 23°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on growth assays of suppressor strains.

claim: In 19 of 20 sequenced strains, at least one non-silent mutation in a splicing factor was identified
source: We then performed whole-genome sequencing (WGS) on the largest of the picked colonies as these were expected to be the strongest suppressors. In 19 of 20 sequenced strains, we were able to identify at least one non-silent mutation in a splicing factor (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing and analysis.

claim: No likely causative mutations in splicing factors were identified in the cs suppressor screen
source: When we carried out a similar experiment aimed at identifying cs suppressors, we were unable to identify any likely causative mutations in splicing factors.
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing of cs suppressor strains.

claim: The identified suppressor mutations tended to fall into two categories: gain of positive charge or substitution with a bulkier side chain
source: Collectively, the identified mutations tended to fall into two categories: gain of positive charge or substitution with a bulkier side chain.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the suppressor mutations identified by WGS.

claim: Gain of positive charge mutations were found in Prp8 (G1868R) as well as the second step factors Slu7 (A24R and N28K) and Prp22 (I1133R)
source: Gain of positive charge mutations were found in Prp8 (G1868R) as well as the second step factors Slu7 (A24R and N28K) and Prp22 (I1133R).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the suppressor mutations.

claim: Amino acids within Prp8 and Prp22 that gained positive charge are proximal to RNA within the spliceosome and addition of charged amino acid side chains may stabilize interactions with the phosphodiester RNA backbone
source: Structurally, amino acids within Prp8 and Prp22 are proximal to RNA within the spliceosome and addition of charged amino acid side chains may stabilize interactions with the phosphodiester RNA backbone.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on structural analysis of the suppressor mutations.

claim: The N-terminus of Slu7 containing A24 and N28 is not resolved in any spliceosome structure and normally contains many negatively charged residues
source: The N-terminus of Slu7 containing A24 and N28 is not resolved in any spliceosome structure to our knowledge and normally contains many negatively charged residues.
evidence: This is based on analysis of spliceosome structures and Slu7 sequence.

claim: The majority of identified suppressors involve a mutation to a bulkier side chain including several in Prp8 (S1594F/Y, V1862L), Prp17 (A251V, G386W), Cef1 (A37V), and Clf1 (T33I)
source: The majority of identified suppressors involve a mutation to a bulkier side chain including several in Prp8 (S1594F/Y, V1862L), Prp17 (A251V, G386W), Cef1 (A37V), and Clf1 (T33I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the suppressor mutations.

claim: The increase in hydrophobic surface area provided by bulky mutations may help to stabilize interactions with nearby proteins, compensating for structural destabilization due to the absence of Fyv6
source: The increase in hydrophobic surface area provided by these mutations may help to stabilize interactions with nearby proteins, compensating for structural destabilization due to the absence of Fyv6.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain how bulky mutations suppress fyv6Δ.

claim: Since Prp8, Prp17, Cef1, and Clf1 are all present during 5'SS cleavage, bulky mutations could destabilize a first step conformation of the spliceosome and suppress phenotypes due to the loss of Fyv6 by facilitating formation of the second step conformation
source: Alternatively, since Prp8, Prp17, Cef1, and Clf1 are all present during 5'SS cleavage, it is possible that these bulky mutations could destabilize a first step conformation of the spliceosome and suppress phenotypes due to the loss of Fyv6 by facilitating formation of the second step conformation.
evidence: This is an alternative model proposed to explain how bulky mutations suppress fyv6Δ.

claim: One suppressor mutation within the U2 snRNA (A25G) was isolated near where the C-terminal domain of Prp22 inserts toward the active site and located beneath the Fyv6 binding site
source: We isolated one suppressor mutation within the U2 snRNA (A25G) near where the C-terminal domain of Prp22 inserts toward the active site and located beneath the Fyv6 binding site.
evidence: This is based on WGS and structural analysis.

claim: Mutation of U2 snRNA nucleotide A25 is not deleterious to growth
source: It has previously been observed that mutation of this specific U2 snRNA nucleotide is not deleterious to growth (McPheeters and Abelson, 1992) and is therefore well tolerated by yeast.
evidence: This is based on a published study.

claim: Suppressor mutations in the U2 snRNP component Rse1 were also observed
source: The mechanism of suppression by this mutation is not clear; however, it is interesting to note that we also observed suppressor mutations in the U2 snRNP component Rse1 (Supplementary file 5) which is released from the spliceosome prior to catalysis.
evidence: This is based on WGS data.

claim: Rse1 mutations always occurred coincident with mutations in other splicing factors
source: The Rse1 mutations always occurred coincident with mutations in other splicing factors.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the WGS data.

claim: Suppressors in factors present prior to or after exon ligation may be able to suppress (or enhance suppression of) fyv6Δ by changing how pre-mRNAs compete for a limited set of splicing factors or by reducing blocks to pre-spliceosome assembly caused by accumulation of stalled complexes
source: It is possible that suppressors in factors present prior to or after exon ligation are able to suppress (or enhance suppression of) fyv6Δ by changing how pre-mRNAs compete for a limited set of splicing factors or by reducing blocks to pre-spliceosome assembly caused by accumulation of stalled complexes (Mendoza-Ochoa et al., 2019; Munding et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain how suppressors in factors not directly involved in the second step can suppress fyv6Δ, based on published work.

claim: Mutations in many different splicing factors including second step factors and the U2 snRNA can be isolated from fyv6Δ suppressor strains
source: Together these data indicate that mutations in many different splicing factors including second step factors and the U2 snRNA can be isolated from fyv6Δ suppressor strains.
evidence: This is a summary of the suppressor screen results.

claim: Several Cef1 mutants were obtained located near the interface between Cef1 and the second step factor Prp17: A37V, M175I, and Q193P
source: In the case of Cef1, we obtained several mutants located near the interface between Cef1 and the second step factor Prp17: A37V, M175I, and Q193P (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on WGS and structural analysis.

claim: The Cef1/Prp17 interface has only been observed in structures of C* and P complex spliceosomes, suggesting its importance for exon ligation
source: This interface has only been observed in structures of C* and P complex spliceosomes, suggesting its importance for exon ligation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that this interface is only present in second step spliceosome structures.

claim: Another mutant of Cef1 A37 – A37P – is able to suppress splicing defects due to a BS adenine to guanosine substitution (BS-G) which causes stalling after 5′ SS cleavage
source: In addition, it has previously been reported that another mutant of Cef1 A37 – A37P – is able to suppress splicing defects due to a BS adenine to guanosine substitution (BS-G) which causes stalling after 5ʹ SS cleavage (Query and Konarska, 2012).
evidence: This is based on a published study.

claim: All of the tested Cef1 mutants could at least weakly suppress the cs phenotype at 23°C
source: We created fyv6Δ shuffle strains for Cef1 and tested each mutant's ability to suppress cs and ts phenotypes (Figure 6D). All of these Cef1 mutants, both those isolated from our suppressor screen and those identified as BS-G suppressors, could at least weakly suppress the cs phenotype at 23°C
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The Cef1 M175I mutant is a particularly strong suppressor of the cs phenotype
source: with our isolated M175I mutant being a particularly strong suppressor.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All of the Cef1 mutants except A37V could suppress the ts phenotype at 37°C to varying degrees
source: In addition, all of the mutants except Cef1 A37V could suppress the ts phenotype at 37°C to varying degrees.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Single point mutants in Cef1 can suppress fyv6Δ growth phenotypes
source: These results confirm that single point mutants in Cef1 can suppress fyv6Δ growth phenotypes
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Cef1 mutant analysis.

claim: At least some BS-G suppressors in Cef1 also suppress fyv6Δ
source: and that at least some BS-G suppressors in Cef1 also suppress fyv6Δ.
evidence: This is based on the observation that Cef1 mutants known to suppress BS-G also suppress fyv6Δ.

claim: Cef1 mutations may stabilize the exon ligation conformation of the spliceosome to favor the second step either when a BS-G is present or Fyv6 is absent
source: A common mechanism could be that these mutations stabilize the exon ligation conformation of the spliceosome to favor the second step either when a BS-G is present or Fyv6 is absent.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the common suppression by Cef1 mutants.

claim: Four of the identified Prp8 suppressor mutations could partially suppress either or both of the cs and ts fyv6Δ phenotypes (S1574Y, V1862L, G1868R, and T1982S)
source: We confirmed that four of the identified Prp8 suppressor mutations could partially suppress either or both of the cs and ts fyv6Δ phenotypes (Figure 6F; S1574Y, V1862L, G1868R, and T1982S).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The Prp8 S1584F mutant was isolated in the suppressor screen but suppression due to this mutant was not observed in the tested strains
source: Even though we isolated the Prp8 S1584F mutant in our screen and this substitution is very similar to S1584Y, we were not able observe suppression due to this mutant in these strains.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Identification of mutants in Prp8 that suppress fyv6Δ is not surprising since many different alleles of Prp8 are known to modulate the conformational equilibrium between the first and second steps
source: Identification of mutants in Prp8 that suppress fyv6Δ is not surprising since many different alleles of Prp8 are known to modulate the conformational equilibrium between the first and second steps (Fica and Nagai, 2017; Liu et al., 2007b; Query and Konarska, 2004) or other steps in splicing.
evidence: This is based on published work on Prp8 mutants.

claim: Suppressors in Prp8 have previously been identified at some of the same positions: V1862A/Y/D and T1982A were identified as suppressors of the U4-cs1 allele or the 5′ SS U2A mutant
source: Indeed, suppressors in Prp8 have previously been identified at some of these same positions: V1862A/Y/D and T1982A were identified as suppressors of, respectively, the U4-cs1 allele (Kuhn and Brow, 2000; Kuhn et al., 1999) or the 5ʹ SS U2A mutant (Siatecka et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on published studies.

claim: Several dominant mutants in the second step factor Prp18 were previously shown to suppress ts phenotypes due to various mutations in Slu7
source: Finally, given our observations with the Cef1 and Prp8 mutants, we wondered about the generality of second step splicing factor suppression. Several dominant mutants in the second step factor Prp18 were previously shown to suppress ts phenotypes due to various mutations in Slu7 (Aronova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a published study.

claim: The Prp18 V191A suppressor of slu7 alleles was able to improve growth at 37°C of fyv6Δ yeast
source: We wondered if these Prp18 mutants would also suppress the ts (or cs) phenotype due to Fyv6 loss. Indeed, the Prp18 V191A suppressor of slu7 alleles was able to improve growth at 37°C of fyv6Δ yeast (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A given second step suppressor mutation may be able to restore splicing activity lost by a variety of mechanisms
source: Together our results from the suppressor analysis support a model in which a given second step suppressor mutation may be able to restore splicing activity lost by a variety of mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that suppressors of different second step defects can also suppress fyv6Δ.

claim: The Prp22 I1133R mutation is located within the C-terminal domain of Prp22 that enters the spliceosome active site and is located proximal to U2 snRNA nucleotide A31
source: The final fyv6Δ suppressor mutation that we studied was the Prp22 I1133R mutant. This mutation is located within the C-terminal domain of Prp22 that enters the spliceosome active site and is located proximal to U2 snRNA nucleotide A31 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Fyv6 bridges over the Prp22-U2 snRNA interaction
source: Fyv6 bridges over this Prp22-U2 snRNA interaction.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The I1133R mutation might stabilize Prp22/U2 snRNA contacts that can compensate for Fyv6 loss and promote exon ligation
source: The I1133R mutation might stabilize Prp22/U2 snRNA contacts that can compensate for Fyv6 loss and promote exon ligation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural location of the mutation.

claim: The Prp22 I1133R mutant is able to weakly suppress both the cs and ts phenotypes in fyv6Δ yeast
source: The Prp22 I1133R mutant is able to weakly suppress both the cs and ts phenotypes in fyv6Δ yeast (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The Prp22 R805A mutant is by itself cs
source: The Prp22 R805A mutant is by itself cs (Schwer and Meszaros, 2000)
evidence: This is based on a published study.

claim: The Prp22 R805A mutant showed a synthetic lethal interaction with fyv6Δ
source: and showed a synthetic lethal interaction with fyv6Δ (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The synthetic lethality of Prp22 R805A and fyv6Δ was only slightly rescued by simultaneously introducing I1133R into Prp22
source: This was only slightly rescued by simultaneously introducing I1133R into Prp22.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Prp22 G810A mutant is viable in the presence and absence of Fyv6 as well as in combination with the I1133R suppressor mutation
source: In contrast, Prp22 G810A mutant is viable in the presence and absence of Fyv6 as well as in combination with the I1133R suppressor mutation (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Prp22 G810A by itself does not suppress the ts fyv6Δ phenotype
source: Prp22 G810A by itself does not suppress the ts fyv6Δ phenotype
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Prp22 G810A/I1133R double mutant is a stronger suppressor of the ts phenotype than either mutant alone
source: however, the Prp22 G810A/I1133R double mutant is a stronger suppressor of the ts phenotype than either mutant alone.
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The additive genetic interactions suggest that the Prp22 fyv6Δ suppressor mutation (I1133R) and the helicase domain mutations (R805A and G810A) impact distinct Prp22 functions
source: These additive genetic interactions suggest that the Prp22 fyv6Δ suppressor mutation (I1133R) and the helicase domain mutations (R805A and G810A) impact distinct Prp22 functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data.

claim: The distinct Prp22 functions could correspond to Prp22's role in promoting exon ligation during the second step (the C-terminal domain mutation) and its role in promoting ATP-dependent mRNA release and proofreading (the helicase domain mutations)
source: These functions could correspond to Prp22's role in promoting exon ligation during the second step (the C-terminal domain mutation) and its role in promoting ATP-dependent mRNA release and proofreading (the helicase domain mutations).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the distinct genetic interactions.

claim: None of the Prp22 mutants activated usage of the SUS1 alternative 3′ SS or enhanced usage of this site beyond what is observed upon Fyv6 deletion
source: We isolated RNA from these strains and analyzed SUS1 splicing by RT-PCR (Figure 7D and E). None of the Prp22 mutants activated usage of the SUS1 alternative 3ʹ SS or enhanced usage of this site beyond what is observed upon Fyv6 deletion.
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The Prp22 helicase mutants, R805A and G810A, both caused an accumulation of unspliced pre-mRNA
source: However, we noticed that the Prp22 helicase mutants, R805A and G810A, both caused an accumulation of unspliced pre-mRNA.
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The accumulation of unspliced pre-mRNA is consistent with Prp22 helicase mutations causing a block during pre-mRNA splicing and having a different effect on splicing than Prp22 I1133R
source: This is consistent with these mutations causing a block during pre-mRNA splicing and having a different effect on splicing than Prp22 I1133R.
evidence: This is inferred from the RT-PCR data.

claim: The block due to the G810A mutation was relieved in the fyv6Δ strains and little pre-mRNA accumulation was observed in the absence of Fyv6
source: Surprisingly, the block due to the G810A mutation was relieved in the fyv6Δ strains and little pre-mRNA accumulation was observed in the absence of Fyv6.
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Fyv6 could act as a negative regulator of splicing of the SUS1 transcript when a Prp22 helicase domain mutant is present
source: This result suggests that Fyv6 could act as a negative regulator of splicing of the SUS1 transcript when a Prp22 helicase domain mutant is present.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that removing Fyv6 relieves the splicing block caused by Prp22 G810A.

claim: Removing Fyv6 restores splicing by activation of the SUS1 BP proximal 3′ SS
source: Removing Fyv6 restores splicing by activation of the SUS1 BP proximal 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is inferred from the RT-PCR data showing relief of the splicing block and use of the alternative 3' SS.

claim: fyv6Δ is deleterious for splicing of the WT ACT1-CUP1 reporter containing consensus SS
source: Consistent with previous results, we found that fyv6Δ is deleterious for splicing of the WT ACT1-CUP1 reporter containing consensus SS.
evidence: This is based on copper tolerance assays shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Copper tolerance was improved when fyv6Δ was combined with Prp22 I1133R
source: Copper tolerance was improved when fyv6Δ was combined with Prp22 I1133R.
evidence: This is based on copper tolerance assays shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Prp22 I1133R was deleterious when Fyv6 was present for the WT ACT1-CUP1 reporter
source: Unexpectedly, Prp22 I1133R was deleterious when Fyv6 was present for this reporter.
evidence: This is based on copper tolerance assays shown in Figure 7G.

claim: If Prp22 I1133R mutant and Fyv6 both promote the second step, then their combination may have an additive, negative effect on splicing due to over-stabilization of the spliceosome conformation
source: If this Prp22 mutant and Fyv6 both promote the second step, then their combination may have an additive, negative effect on splicing due to over-stabilization of this spliceosome conformation.
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the negative effect of combining Prp22 I1133R with Fyv6.

claim: A dramatic increase in copper tolerance was observed when Prp22 contained both the C-terminal domain and helicase mutants (double) for the UAG to gAG reporter
source: Finally, we assayed strains containing a 3ʹ SS UAG to gAG reporter since it was previously shown that Prp22 helicase domain mutants could increase usage of non-consensus 3ʹ SS due to faulty proofreading activity (Figure 7F and G). In agreement with this, we observed a dramatic increase in copper tolerance when Prp22 contained both the C-terminal domain and helicase mutants (double).
evidence: This is based on copper tolerance assays shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Splicing of non-consensus 3′ SS is enhanced both by stabilization of the second step conformation (I1133R) and perturbing mRNA release (G810A)
source: This suggests that splicing of non-consensus 3ʹ SS is enhanced both by stabilization of the second step conformation (I1133R) and perturbing mRNA release (G810A).
evidence: This is inferred from the copper tolerance data for the gAG reporter.

claim: The effect of Prp22 double mutant on non-consensus 3′ SS splicing is Fyv6-dependent since loss of Fyv6 results in very poor copper tolerance of strains containing the gAG reporter
source: This effect on Prp22 is Fyv6-dependent since loss of Fyv6 results in very poor copper tolerance of strains containing the gAG reporter, likely since this 3ʹ SS is located far from the BP (38 nt).
evidence: This is based on copper tolerance assays shown in Figure 7G.

claim: fyv6Δ can be suppressed with a Prp22 C-terminal domain mutant
source: These results show that fyv6Δ can be suppressed with a Prp22 C-terminal domain mutant
evidence: This is a summary of the Prp22 mutant analysis.

claim: Mutations in the Prp22 C-terminal domain can have distinct functional consequences from those located in the helicase domain
source: and that mutations in the Prp22 C-terminal domain can have distinct functional consequences from those located in the helicase domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and biochemical analysis of Prp22 mutants.

claim: Stalling of splicing due to the Prp22 G810A mutant can be relieved by removing Fyv6 and activation of a BP proximal 3′ SS in the case of SUS1
source: In the case of SUS1, stalling of splicing due to the Prp22 G810A mutant can be relieved by removing Fyv6 and activation of a BP proximal 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is a summary of the SUS1 RT-PCR results.

claim: Fyv6 is a second step splicing factor in yeast that promotes usage of BP distal 3′ SS
source: Here, we establish Fyv6 as a second step splicing factor in yeast that promotes usage of BP distal 3ʹ SS.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Structural, genetic, and biochemical studies reveal critical contacts and interactions between Fyv6 and the splicing machinery
source: Structural, genetic, and biochemical studies reveal critical contacts and interactions between Fyv6 and the splicing machinery.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: Yju2/Syf1 interactions need to be disrupted for proper Fyv6 recruitment
source: From these data, we propose that Yju2/Syf1 interactions need to be disrupted for proper Fyv6 recruitment
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural and genetic data.

claim: Fyv6 can enforce the Prp22 dependence of at least some splicing events
source: and that Fyv6 can enforce the Prp22 dependence of at least some splicing events.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the biochemical and genetic data.

claim: Fyv6 is recruited to the C* complex after Prp16-dependent release of Yju2, which exposes the binding site for Fyv6 on Syf1
source: In this model, Fyv6 is recruited to the C* complex after Prp16-dependent release of Yju2, which exposes the binding site for Fyv6 on Syf1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8.

claim: Once bound, Fyv6 (possibly in concert with Slu7 and Prp18) facilitates docking of BP distal 3′ SS into the active site
source: Once bound, Fyv6 (possibly in concert with Slu7 and Prp18) facilitates docking of BP distal 3ʹ SS into the active site.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the absence of Fyv6, the use of BP distal 3′ SS becomes more difficult and BP proximal 3′ SS are favored
source: In the absence of Fyv6, the use of BP distal 3ʹ SS becomes more difficult and BP proximal 3ʹ SS are favored.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8, supported by the RNA-seq and biochemical data.

claim: Under conditions where Fyv6 is absent, the requirement for Prp22 during exon ligation is reduced
source: Under these conditions, the requirement for Prp22 during exon ligation is reduced
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8.

claim: Yju2 may potentially re-bind Syf1 in the absence of Fyv6
source: and Yju2 may also potentially re-bind Syf1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8.

claim: One or both of reduced Prp22 requirement and Yju2 re-binding could contribute to formation of a lower fidelity spliceosome with relaxed sequence constraints for exon ligation
source: One or both of these factors could contribute to formation of a lower fidelity spliceosome with relaxed sequence constraints for exon ligation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8.
